explanations.explanation: This neuron is essentially a “foreign‐script” detector: it lights up on tokens made of non-ASCII/Latin characters (e.g. Korean, Arabic, CJK ideographs or garbled Unicode sequences) and stays low on plain English/ASCII text.

This neuron detects the period (“.”) punctuation token—whether as a decimal point (e.g. 8 .5), an abbreviation or initial (F. Campbell, Nov. 14), acronym separator (U.S.), or sentence/phrase terminator.

This feature flags boilerplate web-page UI text—that is, templated, automatically generated site messages and metadata (placeholder notices, “You are visiting…” prompts, “find”/“follow” links, RSS/feed instructions, customization errors, posted-on dates, etc.).
This neuron is a “dot” detector: it spikes on the period/full‐stop token (whether ending a sentence, marking an abbreviation like “Inc.,” or serving as a decimal point).
This neuron activates whenever the model sees a short, uppercase‐style abbreviation or initialism that ends in a period (e.g. “M.”, “Nov.”, “Inc.”, “No.”, “Sept.”, “Drs.”, etc.).

This neuron fires on chunks of text in non-Latin (especially Indic/Korean/Japanese/etc.) scripts—i.e. inline foreign-language words or dictionary head-entries (often with parenthetical glosses or transliterations).
This neuron fires on the “head” of each phrase or clause—the single content word (verb, noun, adj, adv or even preposition) that carries the core meaning of that segment.

explanations.explanation: This feature fires on the final full stop of a short, standalone header‐style sentence (e.g. news or product title, ad headline, blog intro) — in other words, it marks the end of a self-contained lead line or title.

This neuron is basically a language-agnostic “suffix/affix” detector – it lights up on subword endings or diacritical markers across many scripts (e.g. English “-ER,” Katakana “-ション,” Hindi matras/virama, Korean case particles, Arabic affixes, Thai tone letters, etc.).

This neuron is essentially a subword‐chunk detector for the sequence “et” (and its variants like “-ate,” “-met,” etc.), which recurs in chemical-compound names (e.g. palmate, stearate, betaine) as well as in many proper nouns and place names (Palmetto, Etowah, Roebuck, Demetrius). It flags that little “et” fragment wherever it appears.
